speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the history. To understand the progression of your gait and limb ataxia, have you noticed any changes in your speech, swallowing, or memory over the past year?

speaker: Patient
text: I started having trouble walking recently, and people say I look drunk when I walk. I also feel clumsy in my arms and legs, especially on the right side.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That "drunken" appearance is a classic sign of cerebellar dysfunction. Have you experienced any nausea, vomiting, or double vision that might suggest brainstem involvement, and is there any family history of similar neurological symptoms? Also, tell me if you have noticed any changes in your handwriting or difficulty buttoning your shirt.

REQUEST TEST: MRI Brain with contrast.
REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Cerebellum.

speaker: Doctor
text: With your MRI brain and cerebellum showing normal results, we must look elsewhere for the source of your ataxia. Given your significant medical history, have you ever been diagnosed with a condition like multiple sclerosis, or do you have a known autoimmune disorder? Additionally, have you recently had any severe infections, surgeries, or been exposed to new medications or toxins?

speaker: Patient
text: I have Crohn disease and it has been difficult to control. I have been taking natalizumab for about a year.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) secondary to natalizumab therapy.

I suspect your uncontrolled Crohn's disease and subsequent use of natalizumab (an anti-CD52 antibody) have impaired your immune system, allowing the JC virus to attack the white matter in your brain, causing these ataxia symptoms despite a normal initial MRI. I will need you to undergo a lumbar puncture to detect JC virus DNA in your cerebrospinal fluid for confirmation.
